turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sipho, in you come. I've already written that your back's been sore since the move, about a month.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, Naledi, don't start. Sorry, doc. It's my lower back, it's been really sore, and I'm quite worked up.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit, please. I'm Dr Pillay. Your sister's on reception, but I want your version. When did it start?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks. We moved flats, I packed the bakkie myself, boxes and boxes, it was hectic, and then—
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Week of the move, four weeks on Saturday. He hasn't slept, and the right foot goes numb at work.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I do sleep. I just wake if I roll flat on my back, then I get on my side and I'm fine. And the foot is not numb.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): The pain we agree on. The timing and the foot, you two don't. Where does it sit?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Low, this side, the right, just above the belt. It creeps into the buttock but not down the leg. Could it be my kidney? My uncle had kidney trouble and they called it backache.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Kidneys sit under the ribs, usually with urine symptoms. Any pain when you pass urine, or trouble controlling the bladder?
[SEG0010] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, doc, numbers from outside. Blood pressure was one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, temperature thirty-six point seven.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No, the bladder's fine, no burning and no leaking. Bowels are normal too.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles in the legs, or around the saddle area?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): If I stand too long at the warehouse the right leg feels heavy, tired. I can still feel everything. It's not pins and needles.
[SEG0014] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sunday you said that foot goes dead on the pedals, driving from Epping.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I said tired, not dead. I can feel the pedal. There was a video of a man who woke up and couldn't—
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): That video isn't you. Does the leg give way, or the foot drag?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It holds me. I walked from the taxi rank just now. If it gives way next week, though, what then?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): You come straight in, and the same if you can't pass urine. For the notes, you deny true numbness and Naledi remembers the foot going dead. Have you lost weight?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. The work trousers are looser. Takeaways, skipped suppers, the whole move, so maybe it's that, or maybe—
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been on a scale?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't think I've actually lost weight. My wife says I look the same.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Night sweats?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I checked with the thermometer, it was normal. No sweats either.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): What does the job involve?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Distribution centre in Epping, packing cases of cooldrink, twenty kilos some days. I'm begging them for the scanner. Can they fire me for this?
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): I don't hire and fire. I can write light duty. How bad is the pain, out of ten, and what sets it off?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A six when I lift, a three lying on my side. Bending into the bakkie is the worst. Rest helps, heat helps. My wife—
[SEG0028] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): She rubbed her Voltaren gel on him once. That's hers, for her knee.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, once, I don't use her things. I take brufen myself. Is that going to burn a hole in me?
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me the dose you swallow, and how often.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen. I nearly said two hundred milligrams, but the box is four hundred. One tablet by mouth, twice a day, and a third if the shift runs long. For the back.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is that most days, or hit and miss?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. Some shifts I forget until it's screaming, so I wouldn't swear I stick to twice a day. Two Panado at bedtime as well. I never read the milligrams.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped anything, or still got packets at home?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Myprodol for two days, the codeine one. Made me drowsy, so I stopped. White spasm tablet from the other clinic, never took it, still sealed in the packet.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave it sealed. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Penicillin. A rash when he was small, Mom's story, and we've kept him off it ever since.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I took penicillin for a tooth a few years back and nothing happened. I don't accept that as an allergy. Can a rash-allergy even cause back pain? Sorry.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it can't, and a dose you tolerated later means I won't file it as a known allergy. Call it disputed. Any other illness, old back trouble, operations?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Otherwise I'm well. About five years ago it tweaked after a long shift and settled in a week. No operations. No spine problems in the family, far as I know.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bend forward, and stop where it grabs.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, that's the end of it. Is the disc slipping? Don't dress it up.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain is not a disc slipping. You're tender over the right lower lumbar muscles, and you only flex about halfway. Straight leg raise doesn't set off leg pain on either side. Power, reflexes and sensation in the feet are normal, and there's no swelling or redness.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Do I need an MRI? Medical aid is Discovery, they love a fight. Will I still be allowed to work?

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): No MRI today. My working impression is a mechanical low back strain from the lifting and the move, not a kidney and not a cord problem. I can't completely exclude some disc irritation, but there aren't red flags pushing me that way.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): About the weeks. She says a month, from the move. It was already a niggle while we packed, so before the move, a few weeks. I can't name the day.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The move was the fourteenth. Pain since that week. I'm not changing the file.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then the duration stays roughly three to five weeks, and the start date stays unknown. No point forcing a day.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): What do I do at home? If I pick up a case, am I going to slip a disc? Also the brufen gave me acid once. Is that an ulcer?

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): One episode of heartburn is not an ulcer. Take the ibuprofen with food, four hundred milligrams, no more than three in a day. Keep walking, no bed rest, keep lifts under about ten kilos, and heat is fine.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I need something for work on paper. And if I'm not right in two weeks I know I'm going to spiral.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll write light duties for one week and refer you for physio. If it's not settling in two weeks, we might organise a lumbar x-ray. Come back in two weeks anyway.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the bad things start, the bladder or the numb foot, I don't wait the two weeks, hey?
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Correct. If true numbness, weakness, fever or bladder trouble shows up, come sooner. Naledi will book the two-week visit at reception before you leave.
